title: Förderprogramm: „Open-Access-Publikationsförderung“ | DFG
content:
From Google's English:  "The "Open Access Publication Funding" program provides a fixed grant for the publication of research articles and scholarly books in Open Access. The approved grants can be used to cover the total Open Access publication fees incurred by an institution. With this funding, the DFG fulfills its share of the financial responsibility within the framework of (virtual) information and publication budgets.

Grants of a fixed amount can be applied for for articles and books. The calculation is based on publications resulting from DFG-funded research. In the application year 2027, the grant is €1,400 per article. For open-access books that demonstrably result from a DFG-funded project, up to €5,000 per title can be applied for. The DFG may adjust the grant amount annually. Grants can generally only be applied for by research institutions. Individual researchers are only eligible to apply if they receive DFG funding but are not affiliated with an eligible institution or have additional needs, such as image licenses. The funding period for research institutions is one year."

title: DCAT-US Schema v3.0 | resources.data.gov
content:
"DCAT-US v3.0 is the federal data catalog metadata standard, updated to improve the Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reusability (FAIRness) of federal data. It is a U.S. application profile of the W3C Data Catalog Vocabulary (DCAT) version 3 — not a new or separate standard. This means most DCAT-US v3.0 metadata is valid W3C DCAT 3 metadata, making it easier to share federal data with international catalogs and platforms that understand the W3C standard.

DCAT-US v3.0 was developed collaboratively by the Federal Chief Data Officers Council, the Federal Committee on Statistical Methodology, and the Data.gov team at GSA, drawing on more than a decade of implementation experience with v1.1 and feedback from agencies, data providers, and data users across government. The schema is maintained in a public GitHub repository and governed through a CDO Tiger Team review process to ensure ongoing accuracy and responsiveness to agency needs."

title: OAPEN and Max Planck Society partner to build collection of funded open access books - MPDL
content:
"The OAPEN Foundation is delighted to announce a new partnership with the Max Planck Society (MPG) to build a dedicated collection of open access books funded by more than 80 Max Planck Institutes (MPIs) and research facilities.

The Institutes and research facilities range in expertise, from natural and life sciences to the humanities. The collection will provide MPG with comprehensive oversight of open access books funded by its institutes or centrally via the Max Planck Digital Library (MPDL). Max Planck-affiliated authors will also benefit from increased dissemination of their open access books.

The partnership marks an important step in extending OAPEN’s collection services beyond research funders to support research institutions, helping them to gain greater oversight of their open access book outputs and funded publishing activities.

It also reflects the shared commitment of OAPEN and MPG to strengthening the visibility, discoverability, and long-term accessibility of open access books within the wider open science ecosystem, in Germany and beyond."

title: Memo: Open Access, the Struggle Against Oppression, and the Societal Family Unit – notes, memos, etc.
content:
"Open access, open science, open humanities, open research and open learning is already available in some forms today, though it is often abused because it is manipulated to, again, be of benefit to one’s career with the end goal of a paycheck. It will not be until those who have had the time and place to think, to write, to learn how to teach, also learn to see the extended world around them as part of their family, part of their responsibility, – part of themselves – that knowledge will finally become a true weapon against oppression. Open access, open science, open humanities, open research can fight tyranny of the state, tyranny of the abused family, injustice in the immediate community; it is anti-violence, anti-hate, anti-oppression, and opposes debt in learning.

Open knowledge is a first and major step in the revolution to a society unburdened by the power of the few over the many. While it is true that many already know this, there are very few who have internalized it well enough to act on it."

title: Responsible Research Assessment of Faculty: maximizing quality, transparency, and trustworthiness of scientific research in Research-Performing Organizations
content: Abstract: This multi-interest holder consensus effort highlights the essential influence and responsibility of Research-Performing Organizations (RPOs) in shaping the quality, transparency, and trustworthiness of scientific research. Despite the use of metrics to assess transparency and openness by academic journals and funders, most RPOs do not yet have metrics/indicators or monitoring that address deep-rooted shortcomings in research practice and assessment. These shortcomings manifest as restricted access to research outputs, poor availability of underlying data and materials, infrequent reproducibility checks and direct replications, and ongoing incidents of research misconduct all contributing to erosion of public trust in research. Such issues are exacerbated by institutional incentive structures that reward the number of publications and journal prestige, while neglecting research credibility, societal relevance, and transparent communication. To respond comprehensively to these challenges, our working group reached consensus on six core practices for RPOs to monitor: data, code, and material sharing; open access publishing; prospective study registration; reporting

title: Hundreds of ‘free’ academic journals have started charging fees | Nature
content: "Hundreds of academic journals that launched as free to publish in and free to read have ended up switching to a fee-charging model, according to a study that examined the fate of titles using the diamond open-access (OA) model. The analysis, published as a preprint earlier this year1, identified 440 titles that initially used the diamond OA model — in which publication costs are covered by sources such as institutions, non-profit organizations and libraries, rather than readers and authors — but changed to other publishing models between 2009 and 2026. Of the 440 titles, 369 switched to gold OA, under which authors pay an article-processing charge (APC); 52 changed to hybrid OA, for which subscription-based titles make individual articles free to read for an extra fee; and 19 went entirely behind a paywall. The APCs that the journals began implementing ranged from US$8 to $5,300 and were mostly dependent on the type of publisher: what the authors refer to as ‘professional publishers’ typically started charging higher APCs, whereas research organizations and society publishers mostly started charging lower amounts. title: Green Open Access: where is the index? | chem-bla-ics
content:
"Many universities have green Open Access repositories, like Maastricht University and Radboud University. These repositories are scattered and contrary to FAIR principles, metadata is not shared widely. Of course, prominently, scholarly publishers could provide that information. Any paywalled journal article could have a link to a legal green open access version. It could. It would make total sense if spreading scientific knowledge is your goal. But we live in an alternate universe.

We are relying on third-party indexes. I here briefly describe two options, but love to read blog posts about other alternatives! I am not looking for routes like PubMed Central or Europe PMC that come with huge collections of open-licensed content, including in the FAIR JATS format

It’s really the non-OA-licensed green Open Access that we need to get indexed better."

content:
"New open access regulations will come into force starting in January 2027. The SNSF will continue to fund articles, but publication fees will be capped. It will only support books that are based on SNSF-funded projects.

Since 2018, the SNSF has provided extensive funding for open access articles and books. Unlike most Swiss higher education institutions, it covers publication fees for scientific articles with no upper limit. In contrast to articles, the SNSF also provides funding for books even if they are not the result of an SNSF-funded research project."

title: Implementing Secondary Publication Right in Copyright Law for Green Open Access to Research | McGill Law Journal
content: Abstract: This article argues that, as the Canadian government and governments in peer jurisdictions adopt open access policies requiring researchers to provide free and immediate (embargo-free) public access to research publications resulting from government-funded research projects, the green road to open access (self-archiving) must remain a viable means of complying with these policies. This is essential to ensure that government open access policies do not create an unsustainable dependency on limited government resources. Although the gold road to open access offers immediate access, it often necessitates the payment of article processing fees demanded by publishers. In contrast, the green road to open access does not require payment to publishers for public access to a reliable version of the research publication (the author’s accepted manuscript); however, researchers frequently have limited authority to provide open access to their works in this manner when publishers acquire their copyrights and impose restrictions on republication. title: Toward responsible scientometrics: a lifecycle framework of normative data practices for research evaluation | Scientometrics | Springer Nature Link
content: Abstract: Responsible scientometrics has become a central concern in the context of increasing reliance on bibliometric indicators for research evaluation and policy decision-making. While existing frameworks such as DORA, the Leiden Manifesto, and CoARA emphasize principles of responsible metrics, less attention has been paid to the underlying data practices that condition the validity, transparency, and reproducibility of scientometric studies. This paper argues that responsible scientometrics cannot be achieved solely through improved indicators or evaluation principles; it also depends critically on the normative structuring of data practices across the entire research lifecycle. We propose a lifecycle-based framework that conceptualizes scientometric research as a sequence of interdependent data practices, including data source selection, data retrieval and acquisition, data preprocessing and standardization, data analysis and visualization, data interpretation, data storage and documentation, and data sharing and citation. title: Connecting the Opens leadership series | Zenodo
content: "The Connecting the Opens leadership series explores how university leaders across Europe are connecting Open Science and Open Education in their institutions. Based on interviews conducted by SPARC Europe, the series can inspire more leaders to “connect the opens”. It seeks to empower higher education institutions to address complex challenges through an integrated open knowledge framework. There are six items in the series: The first item focuses on some of the visions and goals that come from university leaders who already connect the opens. A list of key action points wraps up this item. The second item explores the key drivers that are accelerating the shift toward openness in higher education. We examine the interconnected forces shaping this transition: from accessibility, innovation, and economic considerations to policy mandates and broader societal change. By mapping these drivers, the item aims to support stakeholders in understanding not only why openness is advancing, but how these pressures are reshaping the future role of universities. The third item explores the challenges that arise when turning a vision of openness into practice in higher education environments.

title: Connecting the Opens: The Leadership series - SPARC Europe
content:
"European higher education has never been more open – and yet, its various open initiatives are often pursued in isolation, each falling short of its full potential. Across six instalments, SPARC Europe’s Connecting the Opens leadership series has presented a clear strategic proposition: Open Science, Open Education, Open Access and other Opens should not be managed as separate agendas. Connecting them can create synergies that strengthen impact, equity, and efficiency, resulting in a more robust and equitable higher education ecosystem.

The series stems from SPARC Europe’s Connecting the Opens programme, which sets out to broaden the open agenda by making the case for European public universities to connect open science, open education, and other opens. As part of this effort, in 2024 and 2025 we interviewed rectors, chancellors, library directors, deans, and other institutional leaders from across Europe who are driving the Open agenda forward, seeking to better understand how these various “Opens” can be connected in practice. We shared leadership thoughts through a position paper and a series of items."

title: EU advised to do more to support open access - Research Professional News
content:
"The EU and its member states should do more to support open access scholarly publishing, according to a new independent study of OA policies across Europe, published by the European Commission.

Having analysed the policies of 35 European countries, including the 27 EU member states, Daniel Spichtinger, an independent EU research policy specialist and former member of the Commission’s open science unit, concluded that progress towards full OA “has been real but uneven” and “slower than expected”.

“Over more than a decade, EU soft-law instruments, national strategies, funder mandates and, in some cases, national legislation…have undeniably advanced OA,” his report says. “However, they have not produced a coherent, consistent or convergent framework.”

Instead, European countries “continue to differ substantially” on issues such as funding models, copyright and allowed embargo periods before publications must be made openly available.

This matters because the “fragmentation creates complexity for researchers, institutions and funders, especially in cross-border collaboration”, the report says."
snippet: "The EU and its member states should do more to support open access scholarly publishing, according to a new independent study of OA policies across Europe, published by the European Commission.

title: Equity in Orthopaedic Knowledge, Open-Access Trends Among the Top 1,000 Cited Articles in Orthopaedic Surgery - PubMed
content: "Background: Highly cited articles in orthopaedic surgery are important in shaping practice and education. However, their accessibility through open access (OA) remains unclear despite increasing emphasis on equitable research dissemination. Objective: The aim of this study was to evaluate the prevalence of open access among the 1000 most-cited publications pertinent to orthopaedic surgery and examine trends by journal, decade, and study design. It was hypothesized that access to most of the most-cited orthopaedic publications is behind paywalls. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional bibliometric analysis of the top 1000 most-cited orthopaedic surgery journal articles indexed in Scopus from 1980 to 2025. OA status was determined using the Unpaywall criteria adapted by Scopus, which categorizes publications as gold, green, bronze, hybrid, or closed. Descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, and nonparametric comparisons were used to evaluate OA prevalence across article types, journals, and decades. To catalyze this convergence, the open science community is launching a new conference to bring together those working on a new research and research sharing paradigm. The event will focus on knitting together aligned and overlapping initiatives under a common framework that provides pathways for collective action, rather than splintered efforts. Convergence will also offer a wide range of educational and networking opportunities for open science careerists, advocates, innovators, and practitioners. The conference is open to all registrants and accommodations will be made to meet the community’s needs.

Convergence Conference itself will be held in Montreal on June 16-18 2027, immediately following Metascience. Details will be announced soon."

title: Subscription, open access, hybrid – and now AI: AI-induced evidence skew in scholarly work: Accountability in Research: Vol 0, No 0 - Get Access
content: Abstract: Objective Little attention has been paid to how publication and access models influence the evidence that AI systems retrieve, process, and summarize. This article introduces the concept of AI-induced evidence skew, proposes four pathways through which it may arise, and provides a preliminary empirical illustration. Methods Nine widely used large language models (LLMs) were prompted to generate literature-supported content. The accessibility status of the references provided was compared with the percentage of open-access records identified through searches of three scholarly databases. Results AI-induced evidence skew is a structural distortion in AI-assisted evidence synthesis whereby outputs disproportionately represent open-access or otherwise machine-accessible literature. Four proposed pathways are differential representation of literature in training data, retrieval-access constraints, human verification practices, and system- or user-imposed access restrictions. Among 78 verifiable references generated by LLMs, a mean of 95.38% had freely available full text (87.43% were open-access), compared with a mean open-access percentage of 57.83% across scholarly database

title: OER as a High-Impact Practice: From Research to Action — Open Education Association
content:
"Open educational resources (OER) have long been recognized for making course materials more accessible and affordable. Now,  new research from AAC&U  makes the case for understanding OER implementation as something more: a high-impact teaching and learning practice that supports student engagement, persistence, and success.

The research makes an important distinction: realizing the potential of OER is not simply a matter of replacing one set of course materials with another. Outcomes depend on how OER is implemented, including the institutional environment, pedagogical choices, and support available to faculty. That makes the recognition of OER implementation as a high-impact practice not only a milestone, but an opportunity—to make the case for greater institutional support, expanding access to high-impact learning, and strengthening the role of open education in advancing student success.

Join AAC&U and the Open Education Association for a conversation about turning that research into action."

title: Sustaining trusted open access infrastructure: Thank you to our publisher and data user supporters – DOAJ Blog
content:
"DOAJ is supported by a diverse community of organisations that recognise the importance of trusted, open infrastructure for scholarly communication.

Our work depends on sustained investment in our people, systems and infrastructure. We are therefore very grateful to the publishers and data users who choose to support DOAJ and contribute to the costs of maintaining and developing the service.

Publishers that support DOAJ help sustain an infrastructure that provides quality assurance, visibility, and discoverability for open access journals around the world. Our editorial team assesses nearly 9,000 new applications each year, alongside ongoing quality checks and investigations into suspected bad practice. This work helps maintain trust in the journals included in DOAJ and supports the wider community in identifying trusted open access publishing."

title: Diamond Open Access? | Ubiquity Press
content: From Google's English: Abstract: This article adopts the organizational-theoretical concept of path dependency in open access for analysis. According to this concept, open access publishing is no longer described as a single path, but rather two paths must be fundamentally distinguished, and their relationship to one another analyzed. While the commercial path of open access is now perceived as resistant to transformation, hopes are now pinned on a non-profit path (Diamond Open Access), which is organizationally distinct. The efforts to expand non-commercial publishing infrastructures are a reaction to the transformation agreements with the currently dominant publishing oligopoly. Among the numerous undesirable consequences of these agreements are the continued prevalence of hybrid publishing, the largely absent transformation from the subscription model to gold open access journals, the redistribution of acquisition and publication funds among funding institutions to the benefit of the oligopoly, and thus, overall, a deepening of dependence on publishers. title: FAIR Clinics: from principles to practice
content:
"Join us for our half-day event focused on bringing FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) practices to everyday medical research.

This year marks 10 years since the introduction of the FAIR principles. Over the past decade, much has been achieved - but for many researchers, FAIR can still feel abstract and difficult to translate into daily practice. Many recognize its importance but continue to face a simple question Where do I start?

This event is designed to answer exactly that!

We introduce FAIR Clinics - short, hands-on sessions where you will actively work on concrete outputs relevant to your research. The attention is not just on why FAIR matters, but on how to get started in practice."

title: Motivation and concerns regarding the use of preprints among Brazilian health researchers: a survey | medRxiv
content: Abstract: This study aimed to evaluate the motivations and concerns related to preprint use among Brazilian health researchers. A mixed-methods online survey of all 1,596 holders of CNPq Research Productivity Grants in seven health fields was conducted in 2025. The questionnaire was adapted from a survey of bioRxiv authors, translated into Portuguese, and pilot-tested. Closed-ended responses were analyzed descriptively, and free-text responses were grouped by similarity. Overall, 178 researchers accessed the survey (11.2%), and 143 answered items on preprints and were included in the final analysis (9.0% effective response rate). The mean age was 55.9 years, and 88.0% were affiliated with public institutions. Regarding corresponding-author publications over the previous five years, 62.2% of respondents had deposited no preprints, while 37.8% had deposited at least one. Among preprints users, 79.2% agreed that deposition was freely decided by the authors. The main motivations were rapid sharing of findings (69.8%) and obtaining feedback (49.1%). title: Personal Research Ontologies for Personal Open Science | Proceedings of the 14th ACM Collective Intelligence Conference
content: Abstract: As researchers conduct their work, they incrementally construct a personal research ontology: a rich, personal understanding of their field and its phenomena. Yet most of this knowledge remains internalized, with only fragments surfacing in publications. This position paper argues that research is fundamentally an act of personal ontology construction and proposes Personal Open Science (POS), a lightweight method for externalizing a researcher’s personal research ontology for downstream use. The method requires no machine learning or language models, and it centers on the researcher rather than on the publication, the traditional focal unit of Open Science. Building on daily reading habits and a minimal annotation scheme, the approach adds little overhead while producing a structured, explorable representation of a researcher’s interests, influences, and expertise. I demonstrate the method through my own practice of annotating over 45,000 documents across a decade of research. title: We Must Open the Frontier: OSI, OFAI Support Calls for the U.S. to Develop More Open Models – Open Source Initiative
content:
"The Open Source Initiative joins the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) in supporting calls for the U.S. to develop more open models because they promote competition in AI through local control and lower costs. The OFAI is a university-led, collaborative initiative that aims to bend the arc toward human-centered, responsible, transparent, and ethical AI. Led by Carnegie Mellon University, the OFAI includes university representatives from across the country as well as nonprofit voices and individual fellows from industry and government. As the policy lead, we collaborated with other OFAI members to lay out the benefits of Open Source AI and open-weight models in comparison to closed, proprietary ones. 

The statement asserts that the U.S. needs more “focus, investment, and collaboration from the full breadth of the innovation pipeline to accelerate the development of open models. This will require a strategic approach that moves beyond the status quo, bringing together new partners, both technical and non-technical, from across industry, academia, and government.” ..."

title: Open Access in the European Research Area: progress remains uneven as new report calls for more concerted action - Research and innovation
content:
"A new independent expert report published today by the European Commission highlights that, despite notable advancement, the implementation of open access across the European Research Area remains uneven and fragmented. While progress has been made, persistent barriers continue to hinder widespread open access, and further action is needed.

Over the past decade, European Union soft-law measures, national strategies, funder mandates, and, where applicable, national legislation have advanced open access. However, these efforts have not yet produced a coherent framework across the European Research Area, leaving researchers, institutions, and funders to navigate differing policies.

The report provides a snapshot of the current open access landscape, offering policy recommendations to improve access to scientific publications and research data. It draws on an analysis of all 27 EU Member States and eight non-EU countries."

title: Reframing Repositories – COAR
content:
"Scholarly communication is at a crossroads. Scholarly infrastructure has become dangerously concentrated in the hands of a small number of commercial publishers and foreign-controlled platforms, leaving institutions and nations exposed to disruptions they cannot control.

At the same time, the integrity of the scientific record is under acute strain, as AI-generated fabrications, paper mills, and reproducibility failures erode the trust on which science depends and public trust in information is fragile, at precisely the moment when citizens most need reliable access to evidence. Repositories help to address all of these challenges.

To highlight the critical importance of repositories, COAR is publishing a “Narrative Series”. The series provides several compelling, evidence-based portrayals that, taken together, build a powerful case for repositories as essential infrastructure for scholarly communications and the global knowledge commons."

title: Open as Antidote – addressing the big challenges facing science
content:
"This course, called Open as Antidote – addressing the big challenges facing science, was part of the 2026 FORCE11 Scholarly Communication Institute which ran with the theme of ‘FSCI2026: Critical Thinking and evolving open scholarship in the era of AI’

These blog posts are a series of ‘explainer’ pre-reading to start participants thinking about the issues the course considered in relation to the general decline of scholarly publishing. The blog posts in this series considered the problem of questionable research practices, the mechanisms to manage these through corrections and retractions, the problem of university rankings and the uneasy nexus between Open and AI. They finish with some suggestions of where we go from here."

title: Can open science speak qualitative? Rearticulating open science vocabulary for qualitative research
content: Abstract: ‘Open research’ (or ‘open science’) has substantially reshaped conversations surrounding rigor, transparency, and accountability, yet its vocabulary remains largely rooted in quantitative, positivist paradigms. Terms such as reproducibility, replicability, and generalisability are routinely treated as universal markers of research quality, despite their limited epistemological compatibility with many qualitative methodologies. While qualitative scholars have long articulated the limitations this, the rapid emergence of the open research movement creates a new context to synthesise and translate these ideas. Drawing on established traditions and debates, we propose a rearticulation of open research terminology that better reflects interpretive logics and methodological pluralism of many qualitative approaches. Specifically, we advocate for concepts such as ‘traceability’ to replace ‘reproducibility’, ‘transferability’ rather than ‘generalisability’, and ‘dependability’ instead of ‘replicability’. title: Open science interventions to improve reproducibility in science: a narrative review from a behaviour change wheel perspective | Royal Society Open Science | The Royal Society
content: Abstract: Academics, policymakers and other research stakeholders have broadly discussed strategies to improve research reproducibility, with heightened attention given to open science practices. One strand of these discussions adopts a behavioural perspective centred on researchers. This narrative review applied the behaviour change wheel (BCW) framework to analyse 103 interventions evaluated for their effectiveness in improving reproducibility and reproducibility-related practices. We systematically mapped the included interventions across the nine BCW intervention types and seven supporting policy categories, highlighting which mechanisms have been most and least frequently evaluated empirically. We then interpreted these mechanisms using the COM-B behaviour model (capability–opportunity–motivation). The analysis revealed that ‘coercion’ and ‘persuasion’ were the most commonly studied types of intervention, implemented through ‘regulations’ and ‘guidelines’, with active enforcement appearing to be more effective than voluntary adherence.
